Facebook did run on PHP (over 400 billion PHP page views a month in 2010) with MySQL and memcached at very large scale, and its stack was widely imitated. But 'every single one' over-generalises: startups of the same era also used other stacks. The lecture's own next example, Instagram (2010), chose Python/Django, not PHP.
precise_version: Facebook's PHP + MySQL + memcached stack was very widely copied by companies started around 2008-2011, though far from all of them used it (Instagram, for example, chose Django).

note: High Scalability's Dec 2011 write-up of Instagram's own engineering post: 'Growing to 14 million users in just over a year' 'with just 3 Instaneers'. The 14 million is registered users.
A claim about adoption across startups (especially in India); no public data on stack adoption by founding year confirms it. Treat it as the teacher's observation.

Instagram's Dec 2011 stack ran on EC2: nginx, then Django on Gunicorn, PostgreSQL for users, photo metadata and tags, Redis for the main feed, activity feed and sessions, 6 memcached instances for caching, S3 + CloudFront for photos. Background tasks then ran on Gearman, not Celery. Instagram moved to Celery + RabbitMQ later (described at PyCon 2013), and Cassandra does not appear in the 2011 write-up. Redis was a data store for feeds and sessions; memcached was the cache.
precise_version: At the end of year one Instagram ran Django (Gunicorn) behind nginx on AWS EC2, with PostgreSQL as the main database, Redis for feeds and sessions, memcached as the cache, Gearman for background tasks (later replaced by Celery + RabbitMQ) and S3 + CloudFront for photos.

AWS: presigned URLs allow someone to upload a specific object without AWS credentials, use the credentials of the IAM principal that generated them, and are valid until the expiration time. Upload is via a presigned PUT URL or a presigned POST (URL plus form fields).
AWS: with a presigned URL the client uploads directly to the bucket; the URL lets someone upload without having AWS credentials.

The bandwidth and server-load saving is real. But on AWS the extra hop does not mean paying for transfer twice: data in from the internet is not billed, and traffic between EC2 and S3 in the same Region is free (via a VPC gateway endpoint). The cost of the hop is mainly the instances and bandwidth you must provision. Extra charges appear only in specific setups such as NAT gateway processing, cross-AZ hops or cross-Region transfer.
precise_version: Uploading directly to S3 removes a hop, so the upload servers no longer need bandwidth and capacity for every 5 MB image; on AWS the same-Region hop itself is usually not billed twice.

note: AWS does not bill inbound data from the internet ('There is no charge for inbound data transfer across all services in all Regions'), and S3 does not charge for data transferred in from the internet or to AWS services in the same Region. What is billed is data out to the internet, cross-AZ and cross-Region traffic, and per-GB NAT gateway processing. So an extra same-Region hop for an upload usually adds no egress/ingress fee, though it can add NAT or cross-AZ charges depending on the network path. Egress cost matters a lot when serving images, not when receiving uploads.
precise_version: On AWS, inbound internet traffic and same-Region EC2-to-S3 traffic are free; egress to the internet, cross-AZ/cross-Region traffic and NAT gateway processing are what get billed, so check which of these an extra hop adds.

note: AWS: presigned URLs grant time-limited access; validity is set when the URL is generated.

GitHub's flow, as shown, is S3's presigned POST: a form POST with policy fields plus the file. The more common 'presigned URL' is a PUT URL where the signature is in the query string and the body is the raw file. Both are direct-to-S3 uploads.

Correct: the bucket owner pays for storage and requests ('You pay for storing objects in your S3 buckets'), so an open-write bucket is an abuse risk. Today new buckets do not allow public access by default.

The access model is right: AWS calls presigned URLs 'bearer tokens that grant access to those who possess them', usable repeatedly until they expire. However, the backend does not need to ask S3 to create the URL. It signs the URL itself with its own IAM credentials, using bucket, key, method and expiry. Azure says the same about SAS tokens: generated client-side and 'not tracked by Azure Storage in any way'.
precise_version: The backend signs a URL for a specific path with its own credentials and a short expiry; anyone holding that URL can upload to that path until it expires.

note: The flow is right. The 'API call to S3' step is normally local signing by the AWS SDK with the service's credentials (bucket, key, method, expiry), not a network request to S3. S3 checks the signature only when the client uses the URL.
AWS: a presigned URL is limited by the permissions of its creator and lets uploads happen without the client holding AWS credentials, so the backend need not run upload proxies.

Equivalent mechanisms: GCS signed URLs ('limited permission and time to make a request') and Azure shared access signatures. S3's form-field POST is specific to S3 (and GCS's own POST policy), while query-string signed URLs are common to all three.

For presigned POST the URL is the plain bucket endpoint and the authorisation travels in the form fields: 'The upload operation makes an HTTP POST request and requires additional parameters to be sent as part of the request.' (For presigned PUT URLs the signature is in the query string instead.)
'key' is the object key (path) the upload is stored at.

The 'public-read' canned ACL does make the object world-readable. As of Oct 2026, however, new S3 buckets default to Object Ownership 'Bucket owner enforced' (ACLs disabled), and uploads specifying other ACLs fail with 400 AccessControlListNotSupported; Block Public Access is also on by default. Today the usual approach is a private bucket read through a CDN, or a bucket policy, rather than per-object ACLs.

Close but mislabelled. 'policy' is the base64 JSON policy document holding the expiration and the conditions (bucket, key, acl, content-length-range, ...). The signature is a separate field (X-Amz-Signature) computed with the IAM principal's AWS credentials, not with an 'S3 key'. Right that S3 needs no state: it re-verifies the signature and the expiry on each request. Expiry is also capped by the lifetime of the credentials used, e.g. EC2 role credentials of about 6 hours.
precise_version: The 'policy' field carries the expiry and upload conditions, and X-Amz-Signature signs it with the backend's AWS credentials, so S3 can check validity statelessly from the request itself, much like a JWT.

note: X-Amz-Algorithm, X-Amz-Credential, X-Amz-Date and X-Amz-Signature are the SigV4 fields S3 requires in the POST form.

precise_version: Direct-to-storage uploads with signed URLs are the common default for user images because they save server bandwidth, though many services mix them with proxied uploads where validation is needed.
